intro: You searched for "best estate planning near me" because you want expert help arranging your affairs so your wishes are followed and tax is managed. Estate planning brings together wills, trusts, gifts, pensions and powers of attorney, and the right specialist can guide you through those choices. We introduce you to a suitable UK professional who quotes you directly, so you can compare what is offered.
need_heading: What people searching for estate planning usually need
need_lead: Estate planning covers more than a will, and the right adviser helps you see how everything fits together.
needs: You want to make or update a will, but you are unsure whether to use a regulated solicitor or a will writer, and you want to understand the difference.
You need to set up trusts or make gifts to manage inheritance tax, and you want advice that coordinates with your financial adviser.
You want lasting powers of attorney in place so someone you trust can make decisions for you if you lose capacity.
You are planning for care fees or later-life decisions and want to know how your home and savings are treated.
You are dealing with a cross-border estate, perhaps with property in Scotland or abroad, and need someone who practises in the right jurisdiction.
context_heading: Understanding regulation and what "best" means here
context: Writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales, so some will writers are not regulated. Solicitors (regulated by the SRA) and chartered legal executives (regulated by CILEx) are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman. Many specialists are also members of STEP or Solicitors for the Elderly.

When choosing a provider, ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and where your original will is stored. Scotland has its own rules on succession and confirmation, so make sure your adviser practises in the right jurisdiction. Rather than looking for "best", judge for yourself by asking these questions and comparing the answers.

faqs.q: Do I need a solicitor for estate planning?
faqs.a: Not always, because writing a will is not a reserved legal activity in England and Wales. However, solicitors and chartered legal executives are regulated, insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman, which gives you more protection if something goes wrong.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a will writer and a solicitor?
faqs.a: A will writer may not be regulated, while a solicitor is regulated by the SRA and a chartered legal executive by CILEx. Both solicitors and chartered legal executives are insured and covered by the Legal Ombudsman.

faqs.q: How often should I look at my estate plan again?
faqs.a: It is sensible to go over your estate plan regularly, especially after major life events such as marriage, divorce, a birth or a significant change in your finances. Your adviser can tell you what is appropriate for your circumstances.

faqs.q: Can estate planning help with inheritance tax?
faqs.a: Yes, estate planning can bring together wills, trusts and gifts to help manage inheritance tax. Because this often overlaps with financial advice, it is worth checking that your estate planner will coordinate with your financial adviser.

extra_heading: Getting ready for your first estate planning appointment
extra: Before you meet anyone, it helps to write down what you actually want to achieve, such as providing for a partner, protecting a child's inheritance or making sure the right person can act for you. Bring a rough list of what you own and owe, including your home, savings, pensions and any gifts you have already made, because estate planning pulls all of these together rather than looking at a will in isolation.

At a first appointment, expect the specialist to ask about your family, your assets and your existing will, and to explain how trusts, gifts and powers of attorney might fit alongside your wishes. This is your chance to ask whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and where your original will would be stored, as our questions above suggest.

A good first meeting should leave you clearer about your options and about how the specialist will coordinate with your financial adviser, since wills, trusts and pensions often overlap. Take notes, ask for the fee basis in writing, and do not feel pressured to decide on the day.

extra_faqs.q: What should I bring to a first estate planning appointment?
extra_faqs.a: Bring a list of your assets and liabilities, details of any existing will or powers of attorney, and the names of the people you want to provide for. If you have a financial adviser, bring their details too, so the specialist can coordinate.

extra_faqs.q: Will the first appointment cost me anything?
extra_faqs.a: Fees are set by the professional and quoted to you directly, so ask about the fee for an initial meeting before you book. iComply does not charge for the introduction and does not provide the service itself.

extra_faqs.q: How do I judge which estate planning specialist is best for me?
extra_faqs.a: Rather than relying on a label, compare whether they are regulated, whether they hold professional indemnity insurance and how clearly they explain your options. Ask where your original will is stored and how their advice will fit with your financial adviser.
